# Levels

- Route: `/tools/photo-levels`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `photo`
- Slug: `photo-levels`

## Summary

Set input black, input white, midtone gamma and output range per channel against a live histogram. (Photo editing)

## Details

Levels is the direct way to fix a flat photo: pull the input black point up to where the histogram starts, pull the input white point down to where it ends, and the picture uses the full range. Aperture implements it as a layer in the gamma-space tonal stage with five controls for each of four channels, RGB, Red, Green and Blue: Input black, Input white, Midtones (a gamma from 0.1 to 10), Output black and Output white. The three color channels are applied first and the RGB channel last, so a per-channel cast correction and a global contrast stretch live in one layer. A histogram of the current result sits above the sliders and updates with every change, and the layer takes a mask, an opacity and a blend mode like any other.
### What it does
- Adds a Levels layer with Input black, Input white, Midtones, Output black and Output white for the RGB master and for Red, Green and Blue separately.
- Stretches the chosen input range to the chosen output range with a gamma on the midtones, clamping anything outside the input points to the ends.
- Applies the Red, Green and Blue channels first and the RGB channel afterward, so a color cast fix and a contrast fix can be set in one panel.
- Draws a live RGB and luma histogram so the black and white points can be set to the real ends of the data.
- Exports the corrected photo from the original at full resolution with the same per-channel mapping.
### How to use it
1. Drop a photo: The editor opens with the Levels panel and its histogram in front.
2. Set the end points: Drag Input black to where the histogram begins and Input white to where it ends on the RGB channel.
3. Fix a cast and the midtones: Switch to Red, Green or Blue to move one channel's end points, then set Midtones below 1 to darken or above 1 to lighten.
4. Export: Choose a format, quality and size; the server renders the original with the same levels.
### Supported formats
- Input: JPG, PNG, WebP, GIF, HEIC, HEIF, AVIF, TIFF, BMP
- Output: JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, TIFF
- The histogram is computed from the rendered preview; a strong stretch of an 8-bit source can reveal gaps in it.
- Daily limits and file caps depend on the plan; quote them only from the live plan block.
### Technical details
- Per channel the mapping is t = clamp((v - inBlack) / (inWhite - inBlack), 0, 1) followed by out = clamp(t ^ (1 / gamma) x (outWhite - outBlack) + outBlack, 0, 1), with the input span floored at one millionth so equal black and white points cannot divide by zero. All five values are fractions of 0..1, so an 8-bit black point of 26 is 0.102.
- Midtones is a gamma: values above 1 lift the middle (a 0.5 input with gamma 1.2 becomes 0.5612, about 143 of 255) and values below 1 darken it (gamma 0.85 turns 0.5 into 0.4424, about 113), while 0 and 1 stay fixed. It is the same power law as the Gamma entry in the Effects panel and the Gamma slider of the Exposure section.
- Order inside the layer is fixed: red, green and blue are each mapped with their own five values, then the master mapping is applied to all three results. A blue-channel Midtones of 0.85 followed by a master stretch therefore sees the already-darkened blue.
- Output black above 0 and Output white below 1 compress the range instead of stretching it, which is how a matte look is made: Output black 0.08 and Output white 0.97 turn pure black into 0.08 (about 20), pure white into 0.97 (about 247) and leave 0.5 at 0.525.
- The histogram and preview come from your GPU (WebGL2) working on a 1920 px copy of the photo; the exported file is rendered on our server from the original at full resolution with the same levels formula, and preview and export agree within a small documented tolerance, a few 8-bit levels at most, with grain exact.
### When not to use it
Levels cannot bend the tone curve in more than one place, so for an S-curve or a targeted lift of only the three-quarter tones, use the Curves panel. If the photo is underexposed rather than flat, the Exposure sliders work in linear light and scale the image the way the camera would have, which Levels in gamma space does not. For a cast that comes from the lighting, the white balance sliders fix it with two values instead of three channels, and for a one-slider fix the contrast page is faster.
### Use cases
- Rescue a flat scan: Input black 0.1 and Input white 0.9 on RGB stretch a scan whose histogram sits between 26 and 230 to the full range.
- Remove a channel cast: Open the Blue channel and raise Input black until the blue histogram starts where red and green do.
- Matte film look: Output black 0.08 and Output white 0.97, optionally with a slightly lower blue Midtones for a warm shadow.
- Preparing images for print: Output black 0.04 and Output white 0.96 keep tones inside the range a press can hold.
### FAQ
Q: What is the difference between Levels and Curves?
A: Levels is a straight-line stretch with one gamma bend: five numbers per channel. Curves lets you place up to 16 points for any monotone shape. Levels is faster for black and white points and casts; Curves is for contrast shaping in specific tonal zones.
Q: Which channel is applied first?
A: Red, Green and Blue first, each with its own five values, and the RGB master channel last, on the already-corrected channels.
Q: What happens to pixels darker than the input black point?
A: They clip to the output black value, because the normalized value is clamped to 0 before the gamma. The histogram shows them as a spike at the left end, so pull Input black back if that spike grows.
Q: Is Midtones the same as the Gamma slider in Exposure?
A: The math is the same power law, out = in ^ (1 / gamma), but in Levels it runs between the input stretch and the output range on each channel, and it can be set per channel, which the Exposure gamma cannot.
Q: Can I read the slider values as 8-bit numbers?
A: The sliders run from 0 to 1; multiply by 255 to get the familiar 0-255 values. Input black 0.1 is level 26 and Input white 0.9 is level 230.
Q: Does a levels stretch add banding?
A: Stretching an 8-bit source spreads its values apart, so a strong stretch on a flat JPEG can show steps in smooth gradients. Keep the stretch moderate or export as PNG so the steps are not worsened by compression.
